title: Number of Subsequences with Odd Sum
statement:
Given an integer array `nums`, count the subsequences of `nums` whose elements add up to an **odd** number.

A subsequence keeps one or more elements of `nums` in their original order. Two subsequences are different when they use different sets of positions, even if the values they hold are equal. Report the count modulo `10^9 + 7`, as it can be huge.
notes:
## Intuition

Listing all `2^n` subsequences is impossible for `n` up to 10^5, but only the parity of the chosen values matters, and parity makes the count simple.

If every value is even, every sum is even and the answer is `0`. Otherwise fix one odd element `o`. Pair each set of positions that leaves `o` out with the same set plus `o`: the two sums differ by an odd number, so exactly one of them is odd. These pairs cover all `2^n` position sets, the empty one included, so exactly half of them, `2^(n-1)`, have an odd sum. The empty set has sum `0`, so it is never among them.

A state-machine DP that tracks how many subsequences so far have an even or an odd sum reaches the same numbers; the pairing argument skips the table altogether.

## Approach

1. Check whether any element is odd (`hasOdd`). If none is, return `0`.
2. Start `count` at `1` and double it once for each element after the first, reducing modulo `10^9 + 7` each time; this is `2^(n-1)`.
3. Return `count`.

## Example 1, step by step

`nums = [1,1,1]`, so `hasOdd` is true. `count` starts at `1`, becomes `2` at `i = 1` and `4` at `i = 2`. The answer is `4`: the three one-element subsequences (sum 1) and the whole array (sum 3); the three pairs sum to 2.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n): one scan for an odd value and `n - 1` doublings.
- Space: O(1).

## Pitfalls

- Equal values at different positions are different subsequences: `[1,1,1]` has 4 odd-sum subsequences, not 2.
- With no odd value the answer is `0`, not `2^(n-1)`.
- Reduce modulo `10^9 + 7` while doubling: `2^(n-1)` overflows 64-bit integers, and loses precision as a JavaScript number, long before `n = 10^5`.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `MOD` | the modulus `10^9 + 7` |
| `hasOdd` | whether at least one element is odd |
| `count` | `2^i` modulo `MOD` after the step for `i`; `2^(n-1)` at the end |
| `i` | index of the element whose doubling is applied |

narration.3: Only one fact about the values matters: whether at least one of them is odd.
narration.4: With only even values, every sum is even.
narration.5: So no subsequence has an odd sum.
narration.7: count will become 2^(n-1); it starts at 2^0.
narration.8: Double once for every element after the first.
narration.9: Doubling modulo MOD keeps the number small and exact.
narration.11: An odd element splits all position sets into pairs with one odd sum each, so half of the 2^n sets, 2^(n-1), have an odd sum.
